description: Join our team to build an advanced Decision Support System for Mars surface exploration. We combine multi-layered NASA geospatial data with Operations Research to calculate the safest, highest-reward routes for astronauts and autonomous rovers, displayed on a 3D mission planner and a spacesuit visor interface. With a solid Python and GIS architecture already in place, we are looking for teammates to help us finalize the platform and deliver a winning project.
summary: MORPHEUS is a decision-support system that turns NASA orbital data into safe, science-driven walking plans for astronauts on Mars. Using real JPL Mars Trek rasters of Jezero crater (topography, CRISM mineralogy from MRO and THEMIS thermal data from Mars Odyssey), it builds two layered maps: an Objective Map that scores where science is most valuable, and a Risk Map that captures slope, soft sand and radiation exposure. A pathfinding algorithm links candidate sites along routes that never exceed the 18° slope limit. Google OR-Tools then chooses which sites to visit, and in what order, within the suit’s oxygen budget and a radiation-dose limit, with an optional support rover. Crews see the result in an interactive 3D map, a flight plan with an elevation and slope profile, and a helmet heads-up display, and the plan is recomputed in about a second when conditions change, such as during a solar storm. MORPHEUS answers the challenge with a layered, multi-mission map that gives routes, destinations and conditions for completing an EVA quickly and safely. It matters because human explorers on Mars will need every step to be a measured decision, not a guess.
details:
MORPHEUS is a decision-support system for planning astronaut walks (EVAs) on Mars. Orbital maps of Mars are excellent for looking at the planet, but an astronaut leaving a habitat needs answers to three practical questions: where is it worth going, how do I get there safely, and in what order can I visit those places before my oxygen runs out? MORPHEUS turns NASA orbital data into a complete EVA plan that answers all three.

How it works. We focus on a 1.1 × 1.1 km area on the western rim of Jezero crater, placed using the USGS geologic map (SIM 3464). Three GeoTIFF rasters from JPL Mars Trek (topography, CRISM mineral spectra from MRO, THEMIS thermal data from Mars Odyssey) are aligned on a 75 × 75 grid of 15 m cells. From them we build two maps. The Objective Map scores the scientific value of every cell from mineral signal, terrain morphology and thermal properties, and its best safe peaks become 16 candidate waypoints. The Risk Map combines slope, soft sand and radiation exposure, using a sky-view factor to estimate how much shielding the terrain gives. The habitat is placed automatically on flat, firm ground. For every pair of waypoints, a minimum-cost path search finds the safest route, with any cell steeper than 18° strictly forbidden. Walking speed follows Tobler’s hiking function rescaled for Martian gravity, with slowdowns on loose sand. Finally, Google OR-Tools solves an Orienteering Problem: it chooses which sites to visit, and in what order, to maximize science while respecting two hard limits, the suit’s time budget and a maximum radiation dose per EVA. An optional support rover takes the remaining reachable sites.

In the nominal 180-minute scenario, the astronaut visits 8 sites and the rover 3 (11 of 16), covering 1.65 km on foot in 175 minutes with a dose of 61.5 µSv, with a steepest step of 17.7°, below the 18° limit. During a simulated solar storm (dose rate × 2.5), the plan shortens the walk to 108 minutes to stay under the 100 µSv limit (98 µSv) and hands more sites to the rover (5 on foot, 4 by rover).

What the crew sees. A Streamlit web app shows a 3D tactical map, a step-by-step flight plan, the elevation and slope profile of the route, and a helmet heads-up display with compass heading, suit telemetry and local environmental data, drawn over real Perseverance imagery of Jezero. Sliders change the oxygen budget, the slope limit, the science priorities, the solar activity and the dose limit, and the route is recomputed in about a second. Plans export as 3D GeoJSON for GIS tools.

Benefits and impact. MORPHEUS makes the trade-offs of a Mars walk explicit and measurable instead of intuitive: every route comes with its time, distance, slope and dose. The same approach can support mission planners for future crewed missions to Mars, lunar surface operations under Artemis, and analog field campaigns on Earth.

Creativity. Instead of treating navigation as a shortest-path problem, we separate “where to go” (science, the nodes) from “how to get there” (risk, the edges) and solve the whole EVA as an optimization problem that includes human limits: oxygen, slope and radiation.

Factors we considered: crew safety first (hard slope and dose limits), consistency between planned and displayed times, real data instead of synthetic terrain, and honesty about our assumptions, which are documented in the repository.

Tools: Python, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, rasterio, scikit-image, Google OR-Tools, Streamlit, PyDeck and Plotly, with Git/GitHub. No special hardware: it runs on a standard laptop!

Use of AI: We used Claude (Anthropic) as an AI assistant to help review and debug the code, translate the interface into English, and draft the README and slides from our content; the team designed the approach, selected the NASA data and images, and reviewed, tested and approved every change, and no AI was used to create or modify NASA data or branding.
